cells.tense: Right now the aim holds, and you are the one holding it.
cells.ask: Name the goal you're actually steering by, and tell one person why you picked it, before you change anything.
cells.core:
You know which direction you're going. The road hasn't been easy and you've pushed through resistance, but the pushing has a point, and you're the one holding the point. That's rarer than it sounds.

The motion has a destination and the destination is yours. You can turn down the other thing and stay steady doing it, which is how you know the aim is clean. What keeps it going is bearing weight without going rigid — letting the pressure push without bending you off course. Feed that, because the balance holds while it's being used; direction is a practice, not a possession. When the day runs loud, come back to this. You picked this, and the pick is still in your hands. Say what you're steering by to someone, and the grip gets steadier for it.
cells.sheetLine: You know where you're going, and you're the one who chose it.
cells.verb: choosing a direction and holding to it

cells.tense: You are bracing for a future you can't quite force into place.
cells.ask: Say out loud once that the outcome isn't yours to control, then do the next thing on the list anyway.
cells.core:
You're pushing harder than the goal needs. Somewhere ahead everything finally lands the way you want, and you're already standing in that scene — checking, adjusting, bracing. The energy that should be running the direction is spending itself on the bracing.

The result can't be written in advance. Notice what's happening: a delay reads as failure, a detour reads as threat, and the reach keeps stretching past the thing you actually chose. The motion is real; the grip is too tight. The way back is seeing the whole shape of what's actually in front of you, including the part you don't steer. You don't have to drop the goal. Let go of forcing the version of it you can't guarantee.
cells.sheetLine: You're forcing the outcome instead of steering the direction.
cells.verb: choosing a direction and holding to it

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that is already behind you.
cells.ask: Pick one small thing you care about and take one step at it this week, whatever comes of it.
cells.core:
The direction has gone quiet. You can see what needs doing, and nothing in you moves toward it. What's left is standing still, and standing still has started to feel like the plain truth about you instead of where you're planted.

The engine isn't broken. It's empty. So the fix isn't to push harder on the thing that won't move; it's to move at all, even small, and let the motion wake the aim back up. Not proving anything to anybody — letting what's already in you start to show, the way light comes off a thing without effort. Pick one thing you actually care about and take a step. It doesn't have to be the old goal. It just has to be yours.
cells.sheetLine: The direction went quiet, and the quiet is starting to feel like the truth.

cells.tense: You are steering right now without noticing that you are the one steering.
cells.ask: Take one thing you're doing this week and write down that you chose it. Once is enough.
cells.core:
Look at the last month. The way you spent your time, what you said yes and no to, how the week arranged itself — none of that happened to you. It was aimed. There's a shape to it, and the shape has your handwriting on it, even if you've been calling it just the way things go.

That's the drift: the direction is running, and you haven't owned it. You talk about the schedule like it was handed to you and the path like it was already there. The way back in isn't becoming someone new — it's letting the person already steering be visible to themselves, shining without having to prove anything. Start with one item and call it chosen. The rest follows once the pen is back in your hand.
cells.sheetLine: You've been steering this whole time. You just haven't claimed it.
cells.verb: choosing a direction and holding to it
cells.place: where energy is aimed at a goal

attempts.check: The record gives the mechanism and stance, not the person's history, so nothing here should assert what their past held or what they feel underneath — the Too Little cell in particular must not locate any room or event behind the stalling. The reader could object that direction is exactly what they chose and are holding well, so the Unacknowledged cell must stay at 'you're steering and haven't owned it,' never 'you're fooling yourself.' The asks survive a wrong read: each names one visible act that teaches something about where direction currently lives, independent of whether the diagnosis fits. The sentence serving the writer more than them would be any line that makes a nameless stall sound like a verdict on their character, so the Too Little cell stays with the stalled motion itself.
